title: Gargi in the king's hall

lines: A REPLY: NOT FIT FOR INDEPENDENCE.
A WOMAN IN A KING'S HALL.
cards: A quote card goes around a feed, gold letters on pink: where women are honored, the gods rejoice. Signed, Manu. A few posts down, someone answers with another line, also signed Manu: a woman is not fit for independence.
Both lines are real, from the same book. Before we sort them, go back further, to a king's hall where a woman stood up and asked the hardest question in the room.

teach.b: King Janaka of Videha calls the wisest teachers to his court and sets out a thousand cows, gold on their horns, for whoever knows Brahman best. The sage Yajnavalkya tells his student to drive them home. Challengers rise.
Among them is Gargi, a woman, and she rises twice.
The second time she says she has two questions, like two arrows a warrior fits to his bow. All this world is woven on space, warp and weft; what is space woven on?
He answers: on the imperishable, akshara, which many teachers read as Brahman.
Then she turns to the men in the hall: bow to him and go; none of you will beat him. The Upanishad keeps her voice. Now Manu.
Chapter three: where women are honored, the gods rejoice; where they are not, every rite bears no fruit.
Chapter nine: her father guards her in childhood, her husband in youth, her sons in old age; a woman is not fit for independence.
Read whole, the book's picture is honor inside the family's protection, not freedom on her own. So the tradition has more than one page on women. Goddesses worshipped as Shakti, power itself.
A woman asking about Brahman before a king. And a law book that keeps women under guard. Many teachers lift up Gargi; critics quote the guarding verse.
Honored is not the same as free. Read the whole page before you share the verse.

how: Many Hindu teachers point to Gargi's questions to Yajnavalkya in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad when they teach about women and the tradition; the line 'yatra naryastu pujyante' is often quoted on its own at weddings and in speeches, and teachers who read the Manusmriti critically set it beside the chapter-nine verse on guarding women.

games.q: a cousin's wedding speech will quote 'where women are honored, the gods rejoice.' an aunt asks you: is that all Manu says about women? what's the honest answer?
o: it's real, and the same book also limits women. both are in it.
yes, that line is the book's whole view of women.
no, that line was never in Manu at all.
games.why: chapter three honors; chapter nine guards and limits. the line can be said at a wedding, and the honest answer names both.

practice: If there's paper near you, write the name of a woman who taught you something, and under it, the one thing she taught. Then rest your eyes on what you wrote, and read it again on each slow out-breath until the bell.
If it's your way, bow to her in your mind, the way Hindu families touch an elder's feet.

wordCard.voice: The Manusmriti: a book where women are honored in one chapter and kept from independence in another.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Manusmriti 3.56: where women are honored. the verse goes on: there the gods rejoice.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.1 (Janaka's contest and the cows), 3.6 and 3.8 (Gargi questions Yajnavalkya; two questions like arrows; the imperishable, akshara; she tells the brahmins none will defeat him)
Manusmriti 3.55–3.58 (women of the family to be honored and adorned; where women are honored the gods rejoice, 3.56; a family where women grieve soon perishes, 3.57)
